nodes.name: Multiple zeta values
nodes.statement: Multiple zeta values are real numbers, defined for a collection $n_1,\dots,n_r$ of positive integers, with $n_r > 1$, by the nested sum \[ \zeta(n_1,\dots,n_r)=\sum_{0<k_1<k_2<\dots <k_r}\frac{1}{k^{n_1}_1k^{n_2}_2\dots k^{n_r}_r}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Multiple zeta values $\zeta(n_1,\dots,n_r)$ as nested sums over $0<k_1<\dots<k_r$, with $n_r>1$.

nodes.name: Ihara-Kaneko-Zagier conjecture (extended double-shuffle relations)
nodes.statement: A conjecture, due to Ihara, Kaneko and Zagier~\cite{IKZ}, states that all such relations are obtained from the \textit{extended double-shuffle relations}, which, roughly speaking, arise from rewriting the product of two multiple zeta values in two different ways as $\mathbb Q$-linear combinations of other multiple zeta values.
nodes.statement_short: All Q-linear relations among multiple zeta values come from the extended double-shuffle relations.
conclusions: states that all such relations are obtained from the \textit{extended double-shuffle relations}

nodes.statement: Let $\omega_1,\dots,\omega_r$ be a collection of smooth one-forms on a complex manifold $M$, and let $\gamma: [0,1] \rightarrow M$ be a piecewise smooth path. nodes.name: A-elliptic multiple zeta value
nodes.statement: We define the A-elliptic multiple zeta value $I^A(n_1,\dots,n_r;\tau)$\footnote{In \cite{BMMS}, this is denoted by $\omega(n_1,...,n_r)$} to be the coefficient of $\mathrm{ad}^{n_1}(x)(y)\dots\mathrm{ad}^{n_r}(x)(y)$ in the regularized generating series \begin{equation} \lim_{t \to 0}(-2\pi it)^{\mathrm{ad}(x)(y)}\exp\bigg[\int_{\alpha_t^{1-t}}\mathrm{ad}(x)\Omega_{\tau}(\xi,\mathrm{ad}(x)(y))\bigg](-2\pi it)^{-\mathrm{ad}(x)(y)}, \end{equation} where $\alpha_t^{1-t}$ denotes the restriction of the path $\alpha$ to the interval $[t,1-t]$, and for a differential one-form $\omega$, we write \begin{equation} \exp\bigg[\int \omega\bigg]=1+\sum_{k \geq 1}\int \underbrace{\omega\dots\omega}_{\textrm{k-times}}. \end{equation} The regularization of the integral is performed as in~\cite{Del}, Proposition 15.45 (with the order of integration reversed), with respect to the tangent vector $-\frac{\partial}{\partial z}=(-2\pi i)^{-1}\frac{\partial}{\partial \xi}$ at $0$ at the starting point of the path of integration (where $z=e^{2\pi i\xi}$), and with respect to the tangent vector $\frac{\partial}{\partial z}=(2\pi i)^{-1}\frac{\partial}{\partial \xi}$ at $0$ at the endpoint of the path of integration.

nodes.statement: Recall that $A(\tau)$ is defined as \begin{equation} A(\tau)=X(z)^{-1}X(z+1), \end{equation} where $X(z)$ is the unique holomorphic function defined on $\{z \in \mathbb C \, | \, z=u+vi, \ u \mbox{ or } v \in (0,1)\} \subset \mathbb C$, which solves the equation \begin{equation} \mathrm{d} X(z)=-\mathrm{ad}(x)\Omega_{\tau}(\xi,\mathrm{ad}(x))(y) \cdot X(z), \end{equation} and satisfies $X(z) \sim (-2\pi iz)^{-\mathrm{ad}(x)(y)}$, as $z \to 0$, where we choose the principal branch of the logarithm so that $\log(\pm i)=\pm \frac{\pi i}{2}$. Using Picard iteration, and standard properties of iterated integrals (cf.~Section~2.1), we see that $A(\tau)$ equals \begin{align} \bigg(\lim_{t \to 0}(-2\pi it)^{\mathrm{ad}(x)(y)}\exp\bigg[\int_{\alpha_t^{1-t}}(-\mathrm{ad}(x)\Omega_{\tau}(\xi,\mathrm{ad}(x)(y)))\bigg]e^{\pi i\mathrm{ad}(x)(y)}(-2\pi it)^{-\mathrm{ad}(x)(y)}\bigg)^{op}, \end{align} where the superscript $op$ denotes the opposite multiplication on the algebra $\mathbb C \langle\langle x,y\rangle\rangle$, defined by $(f \cdot g)^{op}=g \cdot f$. Now multiplying by $e^{-\pi i\mathrm{ad}(x)(y)}$, the result follows.
nodes.statement_short: Express $A(\tau)$ by Picard iteration as a regularized path-ordered exponential, then multiply by $e^{-\pi i\mathrm{ad}(x)(y)}$.

nodes.name: B-elliptic multiple zeta values
nodes.statement: In~\cite{E}, one also finds a notion of B-elliptic multiple zeta value, which we denote here by $I^B(n_1,\dots,n_r;\tau)$, defined as iterated integrals along the other homology cycle $\beta$ of an elliptic curve. Similar to A-elliptic multiple zeta values, B-elliptic multiple zeta values can be obtained as coefficients of Enriquez's B-associator~\cite{E2}. The modular transformation formula (cf.~\cite{E}, eq.~(26)) \begin{equation} I^B(n_1,\dots,n_r;\tau)=\tau^{-(n_1+\dots+n_r)+r}I^A(n_1,\dots,n_r;-\tau^{-1}) \end{equation} establishes a close connection between A-elliptic and B-elliptic multiple zeta values. A more detailed treatment of B-elliptic multiple zeta values will be given elsewhere.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.6
nodes.statement: We use induction on the set of multi-indices of a fixed length $r$, ordered lexicographically. For $\underline{n}=(0,\dots,0) \in \mathbb N^r$, it is clear that \begin{equation} I^A(0,\dots,0;\tau)=T^{\mathrm{Reg}}(\alpha)_{y^r}. \end{equation} Now let $\underline{n}=(n_1,\dots,n_r)$ be a multi-index of length $r$ and assume the proposition for all multi-indices $\underline{n'}$ such that $\underline{n'} \prec \underline{n}$ in the lexicographical ordering. Now by \eqref{eqn:transl}, we have \begin{equation} I^A(\underline{n};\tau)=(-1)^{n_1+\dots+n_r}\left(T^{\mathrm{Reg}}(\alpha)_w-\sum_{\underline{n'} \prec \underline{n}} c_{\underline{n'}}I^A(\underline{n'};\tau) \right), \end{equation} where $w=yx^{n_1}\dots yx^{n_r}$. The terms on the right hand side of the last equation can be expressed as coefficients of $T^{\mathrm{Reg}}(\alpha)$, by the induction hypothesis, and this ends the proof.

nodes.name: Reflection, shuffle and Fay relations for elliptic double zeta values

nodes.name: Representation-theoretic interpretation of $W_N$
nodes.statement: Moreover, $W_N$ has the following representation-theoretic interpretation. A polynomial $P \in W_N$ can be viewed as a representation $\mathcal{P}$ of the symmetric group $S_3$: the two-dimensional $\mathbb Q$-vector space $\mathcal{P} \subset \mathbb Q[X,Y]$ spanned by $P(X,Y),P(Y,-X-Y)$ is acted upon by $S_3$ by \begin{equation} (12) \mapsto (P(X,Y) \mapsto P(-Y,-X)), \quad (123) \mapsto (P(X,Y) \mapsto P(Y,-X-Y)). \end{equation} Note that $(12)$ acts with trace $0$ and that $(123)$ acts with trace $-1$. Thus, it follows from the elementary representation theory of the symmetric group $S_3$ (cf.~e.g.~\cite{Ser}, Chap.~2) that $\mathcal{P}$ is necessarily isomorphic to the unique irreducible, two-dimensional $S_3$-representation $\mathcal W$. Also, since $P$ has degree $N$, and $\mathbb Q[X,Y]$ is naturally isomorphic to $\bigoplus_{N \geq 0}\mathrm{Sym}^N \mathcal W$, the representation $\mathcal{P}$ can be viewed as a sub-representation of $\mathrm{Sym}^N \mathcal W$. Conversely, given a sub-representation $\mathcal{P}$ of $\mathrm{Sym}^N \mathcal W$ isomorphic to $\mathcal W$, one verifies directly that there exists a unique (up to a non-zero scalar) element $P \in \mathcal{P}$ such that $P \in W_N$.
nodes.statement_short: Elements of $W_N$ correspond to copies of the 2-dimensional irreducible $S_3$-representation inside $\mathrm{Sym}^N$ of it.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.7 (main theorem)
nodes.statement: From Theorem \ref{thm:Fayshuf}, we know that, if $N$ is even \begin{equation} \dim_{\mathbb Q} \mathrm{gr}^{\mathcal{L}}_2\mathcal{EZ}^A_N \leq \dim_{\mathbb Q}\mathrm{FSh}_2(N)=0, \end{equation} which proves the theorem in that case. For odd $N$, we know by Theorem \ref{thm:Fayshuf}, using that $\mathcal{L}_1\mathcal{EZ}^A_N=0$ if $N$ is odd, \begin{equation} \dim_{\mathbb Q}\mathrm{gr}^{\mathcal{L}}_2\mathcal{EZ}^A_N \leq \left\lfloor \frac N3 \right\rfloor+1. \end{equation} On the other hand, by Theorem \ref{thm:linind}, the elliptic double zeta values \begin{equation} I^A(r,N-r;\tau) \quad 0 \leq r \leq k, \end{equation} where $k=\lfloor \frac N3 \rfloor$, are linearly independent over $\mathbb Q$. Therefore we have \begin{equation} \dim_{\mathbb Q}\mathrm{gr}^{\mathcal{L}}_2\mathcal{EZ}^A_N = \left\lfloor \frac N3 \right\rfloor+1, \end{equation} if $N$ is odd. Finally, the map \begin{align} \mathrm{FSh}_2(N)^* &\rightarrow \mathrm{gr}^{\mathcal{L}}_2\mathcal{EZ}^A_N \notag\\ (X^*)^{k-1}(Y^*)^{l-1} &\mapsto I^A(k,l;\tau) \mod \mathcal{L}_1\mathcal{EZ}^A_N \end{align} is surjective by construction, hence an isomorphism, since both sides have the same dimension. nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement: For $\underline{n}=(0,\dots,0) \in \mathbb N^r$, it is clear that \begin{equation} I^A(0,\dots,0;\tau)=T^{\mathrm{Reg}}(\alpha)_{y^r}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Zero multi-index is the coefficient of $y^r$.
nodes.section: 3 Review of elliptic multiple zeta values

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement: Now let $\underline{n}=(n_1,\dots,n_r)$ be a multi-index of length $r$ and assume the proposition for all multi-indices $\underline{n'}$ such that $\underline{n'} \prec \underline{n}$ in the lexicographical ordering. Now by \eqref{eqn:transl}, we have \begin{equation} I^A(\underline{n};\tau)=(-1)^{n_1+\dots+n_r}\left(T^{\mathrm{Reg}}(\alpha)_w-\sum_{\underline{n'} \prec \underline{n}} c_{\underline{n'}}I^A(\underline{n'};\tau) \right), \end{equation} where $w=yx^{n_1}\dots yx^{n_r}$.
nodes.statement_short: Invert the triangular formula (3.21).
nodes.section: 3 Review of elliptic multiple zeta values

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: The terms on the right hand side of the last equation can be expressed as coefficients of $T^{\mathrm{Reg}}(\alpha)$, by the induction hypothesis, and this ends the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the induction hypothesis to the lower terms.
nodes.section: 3 Review of elliptic multiple zeta values

nodes.name: (i) Reflection
nodes.statement: This follows from the reversal of paths formula \eqref{eqn:revpath}, using in addition the parity properties of the functions $f^{(n)}$ (Corollary \ref{cor:fk}).
nodes.statement_short: Reversal of paths plus parity of $f^{(n)}$.
nodes.section: 3 Review of elliptic multiple zeta values

nodes.name: (ii) Shuffle
nodes.statement: This is just a special case of the usual shuffle product property of iterated integrals \eqref{eqn:shuf}.
nodes.statement_short: Special case of the shuffle product.
nodes.section: 3 Review of elliptic multiple zeta values

nodes.statement:

Moreover $\lim_{\varepsilon 	o 0} \Xi^{m,n}_{\varepsilon}(1)=I^A(m,n;	au)$, due to the periodicity of $f^{(n)}$ (Corollary ef{cor:fk}). Now  egin{equation} \Xi^{m,n}_{\varepsilon}(t)=\int_{\varepsilon}^t(\Xi^{m,n}_{\varepsilon})'(x)\mathrm{d} x=\int_{\varepsilon}^t \int_{\varepsilon}^{x}f^{(n)}(\xi_2-x)f^{(m)}(\xi_2)\mathrm{d}\xi_2\mathrm{d} x. \end{equation} Using the Fay identity for the $f^{(k)}$ (Corollary ef{cor:fk}) we get  egin{align} \Xi^{m,n}_{\varepsilon}(t)=\int_{\varepsilon}^t \int_{\varepsilon}^{x}&\left\{ -(-1)^nf^{(m+n)}(x)+\sum_{r=0}^n inom{m-1+r}{m-1}f^{(n-r)}(-x)f^{(m+r)}(\xi_2) ight.

nodes.section: 3 Review of elliptic multiple zeta values

nodes.name: Case $m=n=1$
nodes.statement: If $m=n=1$, then we get $I^A(1,1;\tau)=-2I^A(1,1;\tau)+I^A(0,2;\tau)+2I^A(2,0;\tau)-3\zeta(2)$, which holds by Corollary \ref{cor:diff}.
nodes.statement_short: Check directly via Corollary 3.8.

nodes.name: Case otherwise
nodes.statement:
Otherwise, by i) we can assume that $n 
eq 1$. Choose $\varepsilon>0$ and consider the function  egin{equation} \Xi^{m,n}_{\varepsilon}(x)=\int_{\varepsilon}^{x}f^{(n)}(\xi_2-x)\int_{\varepsilon}^{\xi_2}f^{(m)}(\xi_1)\mathrm{d}\xi_1\mathrm{d}\xi_2, \end{equation} for $x \in [\varepsilon,1]$. Since $n 
eq 1$, $f^{(n)}$ is smooth on all of $[0,1]$, and thus $\Xi^{m,n}_{\varepsilon}$ is smooth as well. Moreover $\lim_{\varepsilon 	o 0} \Xi^{m,n}_{\varepsilon}(1)=I^A(m,n;	au)$, due to the periodicity of $f^{(n)}$ (Corollary ef{cor:fk}). Now  egin{equation} \Xi^{m,n}_{\varepsilon}(t)=\int_{\varepsilon}^t(\Xi^{m,n}_{\varepsilon})'(x)\mathrm{d} x=\int_{\varepsilon}^t \int_{\varepsilon}^{x}f^{(n)}(\xi_2-x)f^{(m)}(\xi_2)\mathrm{d}\xi_2\mathrm{d} x. \end{equation} Using the Fay identity for the $f^{(k)}$ (Corollary ef{cor:fk}) we get  egin{align} \Xi^{m,n}_{\varepsilon}(t)=\int_{\varepsilon}^t \int_{\varepsilon}^{x}&\left\{ -(-1)^nf^{(m+n)}(x)+\sum_{r=0}^n inom{m-1+r}{m-1}f^{(n-r)}(-x)f^{(m+r)}(\xi_2) ight. 
otag \ & \left.+\sum_{r=0}^m inom{n-1+r}{n-1}f^{(n+r)}(\xi_2-x)f^{(m-r)}(x) ight\}\mathrm{d}\xi_2\mathrm{d} x. \end{align} Now we evaluate both sides at $t=1$ and pass to the limit $\varepsilon 	o 0$ to obtain the result.
nodes.statement_short: General case via an auxiliary integral.
nodes.section: 3 Review of elliptic multiple zeta values

nodes.name: Reduce to $n\neq1$
nodes.statement: Otherwise, by i) we can assume that $n \neq 1$.
nodes.statement_short: By reflection, assume $n\neq1$.
nodes.section: 3 Review of elliptic multiple zeta values

nodes.name: Auxiliary function
nodes.statement: Choose $\varepsilon>0$ and consider the function \begin{equation} \Xi^{m,n}_{\varepsilon}(x)=\int_{\varepsilon}^{x}f^{(n)}(\xi_2-x)\int_{\varepsilon}^{\xi_2}f^{(m)}(\xi_1)\mathrm{d}\xi_1\mathrm{d}\xi_2, \end{equation} for $x \in [\varepsilon,1]$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $\Xi^{m,n}_{\varepsilon}$.
nodes.section: 3 Review of elliptic multiple zeta values

nodes.name: Smoothness and limit
nodes.statement: Since $n \neq 1$, $f^{(n)}$ is smooth on all of $[0,1]$, and thus $\Xi^{m,n}_{\varepsilon}$ is smooth as well. Moreover $\lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} \Xi^{m,n}_{\varepsilon}(1)=I^A(m,n;\tau)$, due to the periodicity of $f^{(n)}$ (Corollary \ref{cor:fk}).
nodes.statement_short: $\Xi$ is smooth and its limit at $1$ is $I^A(m,n)$.
nodes.section: 3 Review of elliptic multiple zeta values

nodes.name: Differentiate
nodes.statement: Now \begin{equation} \Xi^{m,n}_{\varepsilon}(t)=\int_{\varepsilon}^t(\Xi^{m,n}_{\varepsilon})'(x)\mathrm{d} x=\int_{\varepsilon}^t \int_{\varepsilon}^{x}f^{(n)}(\xi_2-x)f^{(m)}(\xi_2)\mathrm{d}\xi_2\mathrm{d} x. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Write $\Xi$ as the integral of its derivative.
nodes.section: 3 Review of elliptic multiple zeta values

nodes.name: Apply Fay identity
nodes.statement: Using the Fay identity for the $f^{(k)}$ (Corollary \ref{cor:fk}) we get \begin{align} \Xi^{m,n}_{\varepsilon}(t)=\int_{\varepsilon}^t \int_{\varepsilon}^{x}&\left\{ -(-1)^nf^{(m+n)}(x)+\sum_{r=0}^n\binom{m-1+r}{m-1}f^{(n-r)}(-x)f^{(m+r)}(\xi_2) \right. \notag \\ & \left.+\sum_{r=0}^m\binom{n-1+r}{n-1}f^{(n+r)}(\xi_2-x)f^{(m-r)}(x) \right\}\mathrm{d}\xi_2\mathrm{d} x. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Expand the integrand with the Fay identity.
nodes.section: 3 Review of elliptic multiple zeta values

nodes.name: Take limits
nodes.statement: Now we evaluate both sides at $t=1$ and pass to the limit $\varepsilon \to 0$ to obtain the result.
nodes.statement_short: Evaluate at $t=1$ and let $\varepsilon\to0$.
nodes.section: 3 Review of elliptic multiple zeta values

nodes.name: Spanning series
nodes.statement: By definition, $\mathcal{EZ}^A$ is linearly spanned by the coefficients of the series \begin{equation} \lim_{t \to 0}(-2\pi it)^{\mathrm{ad}(x)(y)}\exp\bigg[\int_{\alpha_t^{1-t}}\mathrm{ad}(x)\Omega_{\tau}(\xi,\mathrm{ad}(x)(y))\bigg](-2\pi it)^{-\mathrm{ad}(x)(y)}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{EZ}^A$ is spanned by coefficients of the generating series.
nodes.section: 4 The dimension of the space of elliptic double zeta values

nodes.name: Group-like
nodes.statement: By \eqref{eqn:comp}, the series \eqref{eqn:genseries} is group-like for the unique coproduct on $\mathbb C \langle \langle x,y \rangle \rangle$ for which $x$ and $y$ are primitive, which is equivalent to its coefficients satisfying the shuffle product formula.
nodes.statement_short: The series is group-like, i.e. shuffle relations hold.
nodes.section: 4 The dimension of the space of elliptic double zeta values

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: But since the elements $\mathrm{ad}^n(x)(y)$ are also primitive, the proposition follows.
nodes.statement_short: Primitivity of $\mathrm{ad}^n(x)(y)$ gives closure under products.
nodes.section: 4 The dimension of the space of elliptic double zeta values

nodes.name: $\widetilde P$ is in FSh
nodes.statement: That $\widetilde{P}$ satisfies the Fay-shuffle equations is seen by a direct computation.
nodes.statement_short: Verify $\widetilde P$ satisfies the equations.
nodes.section: 4 The dimension of the space of elliptic double zeta values

nodes.name: Shape of non-polynomial elements
nodes.statement: On the other hand, from the definition of $\mathrm{FSh}_2(N)$, an element $P(X,Y) \in \mathrm{FSh}_2(N) \setminus \mathrm{FSh}^{pol}_2(N)$ necessarily has the form \begin{equation} a\frac{X^{n-1}}{Y}+b\frac{Y^{n-1}}{X}+Q(X,Y), \end{equation} where $Q(X,Y) \in \mathbb Q[X,Y]$ is some specific polynomial, and $a,b \in \mathbb Q$ are not both equal to zero.
nodes.statement_short: Non-polynomial elements have simple poles with coefficients $a,b$.
nodes.section: 4 The dimension of the space of elliptic double zeta values

nodes.name: Dimension sandwich
nodes.statement: Hence, we have \begin{equation} \dim_{\mathbb Q}\mathrm{FSh}_2(N)^{pol}+1 \leq \dim_{\mathbb Q}\mathrm{FSh}_2(N) \leq \dim_{\mathbb Q}\mathrm{FSh}_2(N)^{pol}+2. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: At most two extra dimensions.
nodes.section: 4 The dimension of the space of elliptic double zeta values

nodes.name: Shuffle forces $a=-b$
nodes.statement: But from the shuffle equation $P(X,Y)+P(Y,X)=0$, one sees that in \eqref{eqn:decomp}, it holds that $a=-b$, and thus $\dim_{\mathbb Q}\mathrm{FSh}_2(N)=\dim_{\mathbb Q}\mathrm{FSh}_2(N)^{pol}+1$.
nodes.statement_short: Shuffle equation leaves exactly one extra dimension.
nodes.section: 4 The dimension of the space of elliptic double zeta values

nodes.name: Decompose $\mathrm{Sym}^N\mathcal W$
nodes.statement: Consider the decomposition \begin{equation} \mathrm{Sym}^N \mathcal W \cong \mathcal W_1 \oplus \dots \oplus \mathcal W_n \end{equation} into irreducible sub-representations.
nodes.statement_short: Decompose into irreducibles.
nodes.section: 4 The dimension of the space of elliptic double zeta values

nodes.name: Count copies of $\mathcal W$
nodes.statement: By the preceding discussion, $\dim_{\mathbb Q} W_N$ is precisely equal to the number of summands in the above decomposition of $\mathrm{Sym}^N \mathcal W$, which are isomorphic to $\mathcal W$.
nodes.statement_short: $\dim W_N$ is the multiplicity of $\mathcal W$.
nodes.section: 4 The dimension of the space of elliptic double zeta values

nodes.name: Character computation
nodes.statement:
Therefore, using character theory (cf.~\cite{Ser}, Theorem~2.4), one sees that  egin{align} \sum_{N \geq 0}\dim_{\mathbb Q} W_N t^N&= rac{1}{6}\left(2\sum_{N \geq 0}(\mathrm{Tr}((1))_{\vert \mathrm{Sym}^N \mathcal W})t^N-2\sum_{N \geq 0}(\mathrm{Tr}((123))_{\vert \mathrm{Sym}^N \mathcal W})t^Night) 
otag\ &= rac{1}{6}\left(2 rac{1}{(1-t)^2}-2 rac{1}{1+t+t^2}ight) 
otag\ &= rac{t}{(1-t)^2(1+t+t^2)} 
otag\ &=\sum_{N \geq 0}\left(\left \lfloor  rac {N+2}{3} ight floor ight)t^{N+1}, \end{align} as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Compute the multiplicity generating function by characters.
nodes.section: 4 The dimension of the space of elliptic double zeta values

nodes.name: (i) implies (ii)
nodes.statement: First note that i) implies ii), as the A-elliptic double zeta values $I^A(r,N-r)$ for $r=0,\dots,k$ are linearly independent, since, by i), their derivatives are.
nodes.statement_short: Independence of derivatives gives independence of values.
nodes.section: 4 The dimension of the space of elliptic double zeta values

nodes.name: Assume a relation
nodes.statement: So assume there exists a relation \begin{align} \sum_{r=0}^k\lambda_r\frac{\partial}{\partial \tau}I^A(r,N-r;\tau)=0. \end{align} with $\lambda_r \in \mathbb Q$ for $r=0,\dots,k$.
nodes.statement_short: Suppose a rational relation among the derivatives.
nodes.section: 4 The dimension of the space of elliptic double zeta values

nodes.name: Expand via Corollary 3.8
nodes.statement: Then \begin{align} 0=\lambda_0(NG_{0}(\tau)I^A(N)&-NG_{N+1}(\tau)I^A(0))+\sum_{r=1}^k\lambda_r\bigg(-(N-r)G_{N-r+1}(\tau)I^A(r) \notag\\ &+rG_{r+1}(\tau)I^A(N-r)-(-1)^rNG_{N+1}(\tau)I^A(0) \notag\\ &+\sum_{s=1}^{N+1}(N-s)\left(\binom{s-1}{r-1}-\binom{s-1}{N-r-1}\right)G_{N+1-s}(\tau)I^A(s)\bigg), \end{align} by Corollary \ref{cor:diff}.
nodes.statement_short: Expand the relation in Eisenstein series.
nodes.section: 4 The dimension of the space of elliptic double zeta values

nodes.name: Coefficient matrix $C_N$
nodes.statement: Denote by $C_N$ the $(k+1) \times (N+3)/2$ matrix whose entry $(C_N)_{r,s}$ is given by \begin{equation} (C_N)_{r,s}=\mbox{Coefficient of $\lambda_rI^A(2s)G_{N+1-2s}(\tau)$ in \eqref{eqn:prematrix}}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Define the coefficient matrix.
nodes.section: 4 The dimension of the space of elliptic double zeta values

nodes.name: Linear system
nodes.statement: Since the Eisenstein series are linearly independent over $\mathbb C$, the existence of rational numbers $\lambda_0,\dots,\lambda_k$ solving \eqref{eqn:diffrel} is equivalent to the row vector $\Lambda_N:=(\lambda_0,\dots,\lambda_k) \in \mathbb Q^{k+1}$ solving \begin{equation} \Lambda_N \cdot C_N=(0,\dots,0). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: By Eisenstein independence, the relation is $\Lambda_NC_N=0$.
nodes.section: 4 The dimension of the space of elliptic double zeta values

nodes.name: Reduce to rank
nodes.statement: Thus if we can prove that the rank of $C_N$ is at least $k+1$, we are done, because then \eqref{eqn:mat} has only the trivial solution.
nodes.statement_short: Suffices to show rank $C_N\ge k+1$.
nodes.section: 4 The dimension of the space of elliptic double zeta values

nodes.name: Reduce to columns
nodes.statement: Also, note that the first row of $C_N$ is equal to $(-N,0,\dots,0,N)$ by \eqref{eqn:prematrix}. Therefore, if we can prove that among the columns of $C_N$ indexed by $s=1,\dots,(N-1)/2$, there are $k$ linearly independent ones, $C_N$ will have rank at least $k+1$. For this, we can clearly assume that $N \geq 3$.
nodes.statement_short: First row is special; suffices to find $k$ independent middle columns.
nodes.section: 4 The dimension of the space of elliptic double zeta values

nodes.name: Submatrix $C'_N$
nodes.statement: To this end, consider, for $N \geq 3$ and $N$ odd, the square submatrix $C'_N$ of $C_N$ consisting of the columns $s=1,2,\dots,k$. Looking at \eqref{eqn:prematrix} and comparing with Corollary \ref{cor:diff}, we see that its entries are given by \begin{align} c'_{N;i,j}=(N-2j-2)\left(\binom{2j+1}{i}-\delta_{2j+1,i}\right), \quad 0 \leq i,j \leq k-1. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Compute entries of the square submatrix $C'_N$.
nodes.section: 4 The dimension of the space of elliptic double zeta values

nodes.name: Reduce to binomial determinant
nodes.statement: Since $N-2j-2 \neq 0$ for every $j$, as $N$ is odd, it is enough to prove that the scaled matrix $M_{k-1}=(m_{i,j})$ with \begin{equation} m_{i,j}=\left(\binom{2j+1}{i}-\delta_{2j+1,i}\right), \quad 0 \leq i,j \leq k-1 \end{equation} is invertible for every $k \geq 1$, which is proved in the appendix (Proposition \ref{prop:app}).
nodes.statement_short: Invertibility of $M_{k-1}$ (Prop. A.1) finishes the proof.
nodes.section: 4 The dimension of the space of elliptic double zeta values

nodes.name: Even $N$
nodes.statement: From Theorem \ref{thm:Fayshuf}, we know that, if $N$ is even \begin{equation} \dim_{\mathbb Q} \mathrm{gr}^{\mathcal{L}}_2\mathcal{EZ}^A_N \leq \dim_{\mathbb Q}\mathrm{FSh}_2(N)=0, \end{equation} which proves the theorem in that case.
nodes.statement_short: Upper bound $0$ from the Fay-shuffle dimension.
nodes.section: 4 The dimension of the space of elliptic double zeta values

nodes.name: Odd $N$
nodes.statement: For odd $N$, we know by Theorem \ref{thm:Fayshuf}, using that $\mathcal{L}_1\mathcal{EZ}^A_N=0$ if $N$ is odd, \begin{equation} \dim_{\mathbb Q}\mathrm{gr}^{\mathcal{L}}_2\mathcal{EZ}^A_N \leq \left\lfloor \frac N3 \right\rfloor+1. \end{equation} On the other hand, by Theorem \ref{thm:linind}, the elliptic double zeta values \begin{equation} I^A(r,N-r;\tau) \quad 0 \leq r \leq k, \end{equation} where $k=\lfloor \frac N3 \rfloor$, are linearly independent over $\mathbb Q$. Therefore we have \begin{equation} \dim_{\mathbb Q}\mathrm{gr}^{\mathcal{L}}_2\mathcal{EZ}^A_N = \left\lfloor \frac N3 \right\rfloor+1, \end{equation} if $N$ is odd.
nodes.statement_short: Matching upper and lower bounds.
nodes.section: 4 The dimension of the space of elliptic double zeta values

nodes.name: Upper bound
nodes.statement: For odd $N$, we know by Theorem \ref{thm:Fayshuf}, using that $\mathcal{L}_1\mathcal{EZ}^A_N=0$ if $N$ is odd, \begin{equation} \dim_{\mathbb Q}\mathrm{gr}^{\mathcal{L}}_2\mathcal{EZ}^A_N \leq \left\lfloor \frac N3 \right\rfloor+1. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Upper bound $\lfloor N/3\rfloor+1$.
nodes.section: 4 The dimension of the space of elliptic double zeta values

nodes.name: Lower bound
nodes.statement: On the other hand, by Theorem \ref{thm:linind}, the elliptic double zeta values \begin{equation} I^A(r,N-r;\tau) \quad 0 \leq r \leq k, \end{equation} where $k=\lfloor \frac N3 \rfloor$, are linearly independent over $\mathbb Q$.
nodes.statement_short: Linear independence of $\lfloor N/3\rfloor+1$ values.
nodes.section: 4 The dimension of the space of elliptic double zeta values

nodes.name: Equality
nodes.statement: Therefore we have \begin{equation} \dim_{\mathbb Q}\mathrm{gr}^{\mathcal{L}}_2\mathcal{EZ}^A_N = \left\lfloor \frac N3 \right\rfloor+1, \end{equation} if $N$ is odd.
nodes.statement_short: Dimension equals $\lfloor N/3\rfloor+1$.
nodes.section: 4 The dimension of the space of elliptic double zeta values

nodes.name: Isomorphism
nodes.statement: Finally, the map \begin{align} \mathrm{FSh}_2(N)^* &\rightarrow \mathrm{gr}^{\mathcal{L}}_2\mathcal{EZ}^A_N \notag\\ (X^*)^{k-1}(Y^*)^{l-1} &\mapsto I^A(k,l;\tau) \mod \mathcal{L}_1\mathcal{EZ}^A_N \end{align} is surjective by construction, hence an isomorphism, since both sides have the same dimension.
nodes.statement_short: Surjection from $\mathrm{FSh}_2(N)^*$ is an isomorphism.
nodes.section: 4 The dimension of the space of elliptic double zeta values

nodes.name: All relations from Fay and shuffle
nodes.statement: Since there are no non-trivial $\mathbb Q$-linear relations between elliptic double zeta values of different weights (cf.~Theorem~\ref{thm:weight}), it follows moreover that all $\mathbb Q$-linear relations in $\mathrm{gr}^{\mathcal{L}}_2\mathcal{EZ}^A_N$ are a consequence of Fay and shuffle relations.
nodes.statement_short: With Theorem 4.6, all relations come from Fay and shuffle.
nodes.section: 4 The dimension of the space of elliptic double zeta values

nodes.name: Case $b\le a/2$
nodes.statement: We first assume that $b\leq a/2$. In that case, the right hand side is equal to \begin{equation} \binom{a-b+1}{a-2b+1}{}_{3}F_{2}\left[\begin{smallmatrix}a-b+1,&-b/2+1/2,&-b/2\\\\&a/2-b+1,&a/2-b+3/2\end{smallmatrix};1\right], \end{equation} where ${}_{3}F_{2}$ is a hypergeometric function (cf.~\cite{B}, Chapter~II). If $b$ is even, we can apply Saalsch"utz's Theorem about ${}_3F_2$ (cf.~\cite{B}, Section~2.2), namely \begin{equation} {}_3F_2\left[\begin{smallmatrix}a,&b,&-n\\\\&c,&a+b+c+1-n\end{smallmatrix};1\right]=\frac{(c-a)_n(c-b)_n}{(c)_n(c-a-b)_n}, \end{equation} where $(m)_k:=m(m+1)\dots(m+k-1)$ denotes the Pochhammer symbol. Hence, \eqref{eqn:app1} is equal to \begin{equation} \binom{a-b+1}{a-2b+1}\frac{(-a/2)_{b/2}(a/2-b/2+1/2)_{b/2}}{(a/2-b+1)_{b/2}(-a/2+b/2-1/2)_{b/2}}=\binom{a}{b}. \end{equation} In the case where $b$ is odd, we can apply Saalsch"utz's Theorem after interchanging $-b/2$ and $-b/2+1/2$ in the argument of ${}_3F_2$ in \eqref{eqn:app1} above, and get the result.
nodes.statement_short: Hypergeometric evaluation when $b\le a/2$.

nodes.name: Hypergeometric form
nodes.statement: We first assume that $b\leq a/2$. In that case, the right hand side is equal to \begin{equation} \binom{a-b+1}{a-2b+1}{}_{3}F_{2}\left[\begin{smallmatrix}a-b+1,&-b/2+1/2,&-b/2\\\\&a/2-b+1,&a/2-b+3/2\end{smallmatrix};1\right], \end{equation} where ${}_{3}F_{2}$ is a hypergeometric function (cf.~\cite{B}, Chapter~II).
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the sum as a ${}_3F_2$ at $1$.

nodes.name: Subcase $b$ even
nodes.statement: If $b$ is even, we can apply Saalsch"utz's Theorem about ${}_3F_2$ (cf.~\cite{B}, Section~2.2), namely \begin{equation} {}_3F_2\left[\begin{smallmatrix}a,&b,&-n\\\\&c,&a+b+c+1-n\end{smallmatrix};1\right]=\frac{(c-a)_n(c-b)_n}{(c)_n(c-a-b)_n}, \end{equation} where $(m)_k:=m(m+1)\dots(m+k-1)$ denotes the Pochhammer symbol. Hence, \eqref{eqn:app1} is equal to \begin{equation} \binom{a-b+1}{a-2b+1}\frac{(-a/2)_{b/2}(a/2-b/2+1/2)_{b/2}}{(a/2-b+1)_{b/2}(-a/2+b/2-1/2)_{b/2}}=\binom{a}{b}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Apply Saalsch\"utz's theorem.
nodes.section: A A binomial determinant

nodes.name: Subcase $b$ odd
nodes.statement: In the case where $b$ is odd, we can apply Saalsch"utz's Theorem after interchanging $-b/2$ and $-b/2+1/2$ in the argument of ${}_3F_2$ in \eqref{eqn:app1} above, and get the result.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Saalsch\"utz after swapping parameters.
nodes.section: A A binomial determinant

nodes.name: Case $b>a/2$
nodes.statement: If $b>a/2$, then the same argument as above works, with $b$ replaced by $a-b$ throughout.
nodes.statement_short: Symmetric case with $b\mapsto a-b$.

nodes.name: Entrywise reformulation
nodes.statement: The assertion of the lemma is equivalent to \begin{align} \binom{2j+1}{i}-\delta_{2j+1,i}=\sum_{k=1}^nl_{i,k}u_{k,j}, \end{align} for all $i,j$ such that $0 \leq i,j \leq n$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to an entrywise binomial identity.

nodes.name: Range $i\ge2j+1$
nodes.statement: For $i \geq 2j+1$, both sides of \eqref{eqn:binom2} are evidently equal to zero.
nodes.statement_short: Both sides vanish.
nodes.section: A A binomial determinant

nodes.name: Case $i=0$
nodes.statement: If $i=0$, then, since $l_{0,k}=\delta_{0,k}$, both sides of \eqref{eqn:binom2} are equal to $1$.
nodes.statement_short: Both sides equal $1$.

nodes.statement: It remains to prove \eqref{eqn:binom2} for $i,j$ such that $0<i<2j+1 \leq n$, i.e. \begin{align} \binom{2j+1}{i}-\delta_{2j+1,i}&=\sum_{k=1}^n\binom{k}{i-k}\binom{2j-k}{k-1}\frac{2j+1}{k} \notag\\ &=\sum_{k=1}^i\binom{k}{i-k}\binom{2j-k}{k-1}\frac{2j+1}{k}. \end{align} Note that $\binom{k}{i-k}$ vanishes for $k > i$.
